title: Disk management
lead: Identify a new disk, distinguish partitions from file systems, and inspect mount points safely. Backups and verifying the target device are essential before changing a real disk.
objectives: Read disks, partitions, file systems, and UUIDs with `lsblk` and `lsblk -f`.
Verify the target and recovery path before running destructive disk commands.

sections.title: Identify disks and partitions
body: Device names vary by machine: a disk may be `/dev/sda`, `/dev/vda`, or `/dev/nvme0n1`; a partition may look like `/dev/sda1`. Do not trust the name alone; verify size, type, and mount point.
`lsblk` displays a tree. `lsblk -f` adds file system type, UUID, and mount points. `fdisk -l` lists partition tables; `blkid` displays file-system identifiers.

commands.what: Lists disks and partitions as a tree.
commands.where: When identifying a new device or inspecting disk status.
commands.why: Shows the relationship between disks, partitions, and mount points.

commands.what: Lists file-system types, UUIDs, and mount points.
commands.where: When matching a partition to an fstab entry.
commands.why: Shows identifiers such as UUIDs for persistent references.

commands.what: Lists partition tables without changing them.
commands.where: When inspecting a partition layout before opening an interactive menu.
commands.why: Provides an overview of disk capacity and partition boundaries.

commands.what: Displays file-system types and UUID values.
commands.why: UUIDs reduce dependence on device-name ordering in fstab.

sections.tip: Start with `lsblk -f`, then use `sudo fdisk -l` if needed. A device name alone is not reliable identification.

sections.title: Partitions and file systems
body: Partitioning divides free disk space into partitions; formatting writes a file system to a selected partition. `mkfs.ext4` and `mkfs.xfs` are common examples. A formatted partition is not automatically accessible as a directory.

In the interactive `fdisk` menu, `p` prints the table, `n` creates a partition, and `w` writes changes. Writing to the wrong disk can destroy data. Practice only on a disposable virtual disk with a recovery plan.

commands.what: Creates an ext4 file system on a partition and erases existing data.
commands.where: Only on a verified, empty partition with a backup.
commands.why: Linux needs a file system to store files on the partition.

commands.what: Creates XFS on a partition and erases existing data.
commands.where: On an empty test partition when XFS is intended.
commands.why: Choose a file-system type that fits the workload and distribution.

sections.danger: `mkfs` or `w` in `fdisk` can destroy data. Never try these on the system disk, a real USB drive, or an unverified device. The VM tasks in this module only read information and do not format anything.

sections.title: Mounting and persistent configuration
body: `mount` attaches a file system to a directory; `umount` detaches it. Create the mount point first. `findmnt` shows current mounts, while `df -hT` shows file-system type and usage.

Use `/etc/fstab` for mounts that should persist across reboots. Prefer UUIDs over device names. Its fields are source, target, type, options, dump, and fsck order. `nofail` can keep a missing optional disk from blocking boot; choose options for the actual situation.

commands.what: Shows mounted file systems; with a device and directory, it mounts one.
commands.where: When inspecting current mounts or performing an approved mount operation.
commands.why: Linux exposes disk contents through directories.

commands.where: Before removing external storage or beginning maintenance.
commands.why: Allows writes to finish and the file system to be detached safely.

commands.what: Lists mounted file systems with their source and target.
commands.where: When verifying where a partition is mounted.
commands.why: Presents the mount table in a readable form.

sections.tip: Back up `/etc/fstab` before editing. Afterward, use `sudo mount -a` to check the syntax instead of rebooting immediately; it can perform mounts.

t01.text: List the sample disk workspace in the simulator with `ls ~/disklab`; inspect the real disk tree in your own VM.
t01.hint: `lsblk` shows the real device tree; here you are only listing sample files.

t02.text: Run `df -h` in the simulator and inspect the disk usage report.

t03.text: Read the sample disk tree with `cat ~/disklab/lsblk.txt`. What is the second disk called?

t05.text: Predict: which UUID does the sample fstab use for `/data`? Verify with `grep data ~/disklab/fstab.sample`.
t05.hint: The UUID follows `UUID=` at the start of the line.

t06.text: Remove the incorrect or temporary sample entry in `~/disklab/fstab.tmp`.
t06.hint: Check the path and name, then run `rm ~/disklab/fstab.tmp`.

t07.text: Mini project: write a mount plan for `/data` with a UUID and the `nofail` option to `~/disklab/mount-plan.txt`.

t08.text: Challenge: make a backup of the sample fstab at `~/disklab/fstab.backup`.

t09.text: Ticket: "The new disk is not visible." Write in the support note that `lsblk` should be checked first, followed by `df -hT`.
t09.hint: Save both commands in a text line with `echo`.

vm.intro: These tasks only read disk information; they do not change partition tables or file systems. Run them in your VM and review the output before sharing device names.

v01.title: Disk and file-system tree
v01.text: List disks, partitions, and file-system types. Check mount points instead of guessing which disk is the system disk from its name.

blocks.expected: NAME FSTYPE FSVER LABEL UUID FSAVAIL FSUSE% MOUNTPOINTS

differs: Columns and device names vary by distribution; you may see `sda`, `vda`, or `nvme0n1`.
A blank extra disk may have empty FSTYPE and MOUNTPOINTS columns.

v02.title: Mounted space usage
v02.text: Show the size and usage of mounted file systems, including their types.

blocks.expected: Filesystem Type Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on

differs: Containers and WSL may show multiple `overlay` or `tmpfs` lines.
Pay particular attention to the Use% value for mount point `/`.

v03.title: Verify the root mount
v03.text: Find the source and file-system type used to mount the root directory (`/`).
differs: The source may be `/dev/mapper/...` or `/dev/nvme0n1p...`; the sample output need not match exactly.
This command does not change the disk.

q1.q: Which command displays disks and partitions as a tree?

q2.q: Which command can destroy existing data?
q2.explain: `mkfs` writes a new file system to the selected device and erases existing data.

q3.q: What do we call the directory through which a mounted file system is accessed?
q3.explain: A mount point is the path in the Linux directory tree where a file system is accessible.

q4.q: Which identifier is generally more persistent in fstab than a device name?
q4.explain: A UUID identifies the file system even if device names change.

summary: `lsblk -f` shows the disk tree along with file-system types and UUIDs.
`mkfs` erases data; use it only on a verified empty test device with a backup.
`mount` attaches, `umount` detaches; `findmnt` and `df -hT` are read-only checks.
Use UUIDs in `/etc/fstab`, back up the file, and verify changes carefully.

glossary.meaning: A region of a physical or virtual disk defined in its partition table.
The structure that defines how files and directories are stored on a partition.
The directory through which a mounted file system is accessed.
A unique identifier for a file system.
